papers.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
papers.abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

papers.title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

papers.title: On the Complexity of Envy Cycle Elimination
papers.abstract: The envy cycle elimination (ECE) algorithm is a fundamental algorithm for the fair allocation of indivisible goods, guaranteeing an allocation that is envy-free up to one good under arbitrary monotone utilities. We show that the ECE algorithm can be implemented in $O(nm)$ time for $n$ agents and $m$ goods, and establish the tightness of this bound.

papers.title: Sharp Complexity Thresholds for Network Cournot Competition
papers.abstract: We determine the approximation complexity of network Cournot equilibrium as a function of demand degree and the number of firms sharing a market. For common, nonincreasing concave polynomial inverse demands, convex quadratic costs of firms' allocation vectors, and rational total capacities, high-precision approximation is polynomial-time solvable for cubic demands, regardless of market size. Quartic demands remain tractable when each market has at most three firms, and quintic demands remain tractable with at most two. These thresholds are exact: approximation at a fixed positive profit-regret tolerance is PPAD-hard for quartic demands with four firms per market, quintic demands with three, and sextic demands with two. Each hardness result uses one fixed demand curve in every market, a constant number of markets per firm, and globally nondecreasing strongly convex quadratic costs. We also give a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary-degree nonincreasing concave polynomial demands when each firm's convex polynomial cost depends only on its total production. The algorithm applies to arbitrary access graphs and permits firm-specific inverse demands. Its running time is polynomial in the input size and the logarithm of the inverse accuracy. The algorithm assigns one marginal charge to each firm and adjusts the charges until each firm's total sales approximate the quantity it would produce at that charge.

papers.title: Uncertainty, bias and the institution bootstrapping problem
papers.abstract: Institutions play a critical role in enabling communities to manage common-pool resources and avert tragedies of the commons. However, a fundamental issue arises: Individuals typically perceive participation as advantageous only after an institution is established, creating a paradox: How can institutions form if no one will join before a critical mass exists? We term this conundrum the institution bootstrapping problem and propose that misperception, specifically, agents' erroneous belief that an institution already exists, could resolve this paradox. By integrating well-documented psychological phenomena, including cognitive biases, probability distortion, and perceptual noise, into a game-theoretic framework, we demonstrate how these factors collectively mitigate the bootstrapping problem. Notably, unbiased perceptual noise (e.g., noise arising from agents' heterogeneous physical or social contexts) drastically reduces the critical mass of cooperators required for institutional emergence. This effect intensifies with greater diversity of perceptions. We explain this counter-intuitive result through asymmetric boundary conditions: proportional underestimation of low-probability sanctions produces distinct outcomes compared to equivalent overestimation. Furthermore, the type of perceptual distortion, proportional versus absolute, yields qualitatively different evolutionary pathways. These findings challenge conventional assumptions about rationality in institutional design, highlighting how "noisy" cognition can paradoxically enhance cooperation. Finally, we contextualize these insights within broader discussions of multi-agent system design and collective action. Our analysis underscores the importance of incorporating human-like cognitive constraints, not just idealized rationality, into models of institutional emergence and resilience.

papers.title: Expanding and Evaluating the Applicability of Safe Pareto Improvements
papers.abstract: Even when players can make credible joint commitments in games, disagreement about the game's default outcome (e.g., about equilibrium selection) can prevent them from agreeing on any particular payoff profile. We study safe Pareto improvements (SPIs): commitments that sidestep this obstacle by inducing a new game that is isomorphic to the original (after iteratively removing strictly dominated actions) but entrywise Pareto better. We do so by constructing token games: cheap-talk games rendered meaningful by commitments to take payoff-relevant actions (in prior work, strategies in the original game) as a function of the token outcome. Since these token games preserve the original game's strategic structure, players should expect them to be played isomorphically and hence agree that they Pareto improve on the original. In this work, we study token game SPIs under three additional commitment abilities: (1) burning utility, (2) transferring utility between players, and (3) transferring utility with an outside party conditional on the token outcome (e.g., via insurance-like contracts). We characterize when SPIs exist in each case and give efficient algorithms for optimizing over them. Finally, we propose evaluating SPI frameworks by how often they enable SPIs in randomly generated games. In such experiments, our methods substantially outperform prior work.

papers.title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores
papers.abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $\beta \ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $\beta$-TEF1 allocation.

papers.title: Ordinal Hegselmann-Krause Systems
papers.abstract: We study opinion formation in the popular Hegselmann-Krause model when agents replace the traditional averaging update by a median update or more general ordinal aggregation methods. We analyze the convergence properties of synchronous and asynchronous dynamics. For asynchronous dynamics, we show that every HKS with a $1$-Lipschitz ordinal aggregation function converges in worst-case time $\mathcal{O}(n^4)$. For the special case of median aggregation and for the family of $k\textsf{-large}$ aggregation functions, in which agents select the $k$-th largest opinion in their neighborhood, we obtain sharper bounds of $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$. For general ordinal aggregation, some sequence of $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ updates reaches an equilibrium from every initial state. Nevertheless, other update sequences may cycle, and uniform random activation can require exponentially many updates with overwhelming probability. For synchronous dynamics, we obtain a tight characterization. Ordinal aggregation functions satisfying the $1$-Lipschitz condition are shown to guarantee convergence in linear time. This result applies to many natural examples such as minimum, maximum, median, and $k\textsf{-large}$ functions. When the Lipschitz condition is violated, there exist instances in which synchronous dynamics do not converge at all.

papers.title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
papers.abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.

papers.title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
papers.abstract: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.

papers.title: An Anchor-and-Propagate Scheme for Certified $O(n^2)$ Computation of Shapley Vectors in Cooperative Product Games
papers.abstract:
For a general cooperative game, the Shapley values of the players need not be related, but for cooperative product games they are closely linked; identifying and exploiting these relations is one purpose of this study. We consider a network of \(n\) devices that participate independently with probabilities \(p_1,\dots,p_n\), giving the plausibility game \(T(S)=1-\prod_{i\in S}(1-p_i)\), whose Shapley values are \(\phi_i=p_i\int_0^1\prod_{j
e i}(1-p_jt)\,dt\). Since \(T=1-w\) for the product game \(w(S)=\prod_{i\in S}(1-p_i)\), the results transfer to product games with factors in \([0,1]\). Our main contribution is an \emph{anchor-and-propagate} scheme: once \(\phi_1\) is computed exactly, the exact identities \(\phi_i=c_i\phi_1+p_i(p_i-p_1)B_i\) and \(\phi_i=\phi_1+(p_i-p_1)J_i\), with \(c_i=p_i/p_1\) and one-dimensional integrals \(B_i\le	frac12J_i\), give the remaining \(n-1\) values in \(O(n)\) total time with certified error bounds. For small \(S_i=\sum_{j
e1,i}p_j\) we use a truncated Bonferroni expansion of \(B_i\); for large \(S_i\), a new estimator with relative error \(O(m_i^2/S_i^2)\), \(m_i=\max_{j
e1,i}p_j\). The anchor is computed by Gauss--Legendre quadrature in \(O(n^2)\) operations or, without irrational nodes, exactly by polynomial expansion. The whole vector costs \(	frac32n^2+O(n)\) operations, about half the exact baseline and less than QuadraSHAP. For \(n=100\), the scheme uses \(1.8	imes10^4\) operations with errors below \(3.4	imes10^{-7}\), within a certified bound of \(2.1	imes10^{-6}\); permutation sampling (Castro et al.) needs \(4	imes10^7\) operations for an error of \(7.9	imes10^{-4}\), controlled only in probability. We also give an anchor-free closed-form approximation with an explicit error bound, and a self-contained derivation of Shapley's formula using combinatorial identities and the Beta function.

papers.title: Counterexamples to EFX for Submodular and Subadditive Valuations
papers.abstract: The existence of EFX allocations is a fundamental question in fair division. In this paper, we construct a three-agent, eight-good instance with monotone subadditive valuations such that no allocation satisfies $\alpha$-EFX for any $\alpha > \frac{1}{\sqrt[6]{2}} \approx 0.89$. We also provide a closely related three-agent, eight-good instance with submodular (in fact weighted coverage) valuations for which no EFX allocation exists. A key feature of our construction is its symmetry: the agents' valuations are identical up to a relabeling of the goods. Thus, EFX can fail even when agents differ only in how the goods are labeled. This symmetry makes the counterexamples compact and human-verifiable, yielding simple combinatorial obstructions to the existence of EFX.

papers.title: Fair Division Under Boolean Valuations: Beyond Normalization
papers.abstract: We study fair division of indivisible items when agents have arbitrary two-level preferences: the value of each agent for any set of items is Boolean, which need not be monotone or additive. Notably, we do not impose the standard assumption of normalization, i.e., different agents may value the empty set at different Boolean levels. Since the preferences are nonmonotone, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) each admit several variants, depending on which items are tested for removal and whether they are removed from the envious agent's bundle or the envied agent's bundle. This paper investigates the existence of these variants of EF1 and EFX, on their own and together with economic efficiency, incentive compatibility, feasibility constraints, and lottery-based randomization. Our paper presents a wide range of positive and negative results that collectively highlight an interesting phenomenon: the landscape of achievable guarantees depends crucially on the number of normalized agents, who value the empty bundle at the lower Boolean level.
